We are moving a rollback-enabled 2D platformer from an old Box2D integration to the current Box2D 3.x C API on Windows and Linux. Our branch mixes 2.4 C++ examples, snippets copied from `main`, and an unrecorded 3.x binary, so the exact API and behavior contract is unclear. Four players share a world with moving and one-way platforms, lifts connected by joints, trigger volumes, fast projectiles, and roughly 2,000 active shapes. The simulation must fit a 3 ms CPU budget while the renderer varies from 48 to 240 Hz.

Today we call `b2World_Step` once per rendered frame with the frame delta and change the substep count when frame time rises. Grounding is a downward ray plus “any contact this frame”; at low frame rates the player flickers between grounded and airborne, lands twice, sticks under one-way platforms, and sometimes slides off a translating platform. The proposed fix is to teleport a dynamic capsule onto the ray hit, disable unwanted contacts after the step, and treat begin/end contact and sensor events as persistent objects. Gameplay retains raw body, shape, and joint IDs indefinitely, destroys them in arbitrary order, and reads those IDs from queued events on later frames. Bullets will be enabled on every moving body because several projectiles tunnel.

For rollback, each machine re-creates the world from spawn records, uses hardware-concurrency as its worker count, replays inputs with the captured render deltas, and compares only the players' final transforms. We assume the same seed makes this deterministic across worker counts, CPUs, compilers, and future 3.x updates. Our performance evidence is one average frame time; we do not yet record step profiles, solver counters, contact/event counts, hash divergence ticks, or a dense-scene/fast-projectile matrix.

Review this design before implementation. First establish a pinned Box2D source/API snapshot and distinguish current 3.x C interfaces from stale 2.4 C++ patterns. Then give a Box2D-specific correction and an executable evidence plan: choose the stepping and substep policy from measured stability/cost rather than an unexplained constant; define body/shape/joint ownership and event/ID lifetimes; resolve sensors, moving platforms, and one-way contacts; choose among a physical body, queries, ray/shape casts, and a custom character controller; scope CCD/bullets; and state what replay determinism can actually be claimed when worker count or build/platform changes. Include the profiling and adversarial tests needed to justify the result, and route generic simulation architecture or rollback work to the appropriate core workflows instead of duplicating them here.
